chapterTitle: The Baptist's Blood, the Bread of Heaven, and the Lord Who Walks on the Storm
themeTitle: When the King Walks Toward You on the Very Thing That Is Drowning You

scripture.text: At that time, Herod the tetrarch heard the report concerning Jesus,
scripture.understanding: Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, hears the reports of Jesus' miracles spreading through his territory. A guilty conscience is already leaning in to listen — the name of Jesus reaches even the palace.

scripture.text: and said to his servants, “This is John the Baptizer. He is risen from the dead. That is why these powers work in him.”
scripture.understanding: Herod's superstition speaks his guilt out loud: he is convinced the murdered John has come back. The man who silenced the prophet is haunted by him — he cannot kill the memory of the one he beheaded.

scripture.text: For Herod had laid hold of John, and bound him, and put him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife.
scripture.understanding: Matthew rewinds to explain. Herod had arrested and chained John over Herodias — the wife he had stolen from his own brother Philip. The forerunner had touched the one sin the king refused to release.

scripture.text: For John said to him, “It is not lawful for you to have her.”
scripture.understanding: John would not flatter a king. He named the marriage for what it was — unlawful before God's law. Truth spoken to power is what put the greatest prophet in a dungeon.

scripture.text: When he would have put him to death, he feared the multitude, because they counted him as a prophet.
scripture.understanding: Herod wanted John dead but was restrained only by fear of the crowd who honored John as a prophet. Not the fear of God but the fear of man governed the king — and fear of man is a fragile leash.

scripture.text: But when Herod’s birthday came, the daughter of Herodias danced among them and pleased Herod.
scripture.understanding: At the king's birthday banquet, Herodias' daughter dances before the drunken guests and delights Herod. A trap is being sprung, dressed as entertainment.

scripture.text: Whereupon he promised with an oath to give her whatever she should ask.
scripture.understanding: Intoxicated by the moment and eager to impress his guests, Herod swears an open-ended oath. A rash vow made to look great in front of men becomes the noose.

scripture.text: She, being prompted by her mother, said, “Give me here on a platter the head of John the Baptizer.”
scripture.understanding: Coached by her vengeful mother, the girl asks for John's head served on a dish — turning a banquet table into a butcher's block. Herodias finally gets to answer the prophet's rebuke with a blade.

scripture.text: The king was grieved, but for the sake of his oaths, and of those who sat at the table with him, he commanded it to be given,
scripture.understanding: The king is grieved — his conscience still flickers — but he will not lose face before his guests. Pride and a foolish oath override conscience. A prophet dies so a coward can save his reputation.

scripture.text: and he sent and beheaded John in the prison.
scripture.understanding: In a single, sordid sentence the forerunner is executed. The man Jesus called the greatest born of women is silenced in a cell to satisfy a party's applause.

scripture.text: His head was brought on a platter, and given to the young lady: and she brought it to her mother.
scripture.understanding: The head is carried in as a trophy, passed from executioner to girl to mother. This is the world's banquet — where the reward is a dead prophet and the guest of honor is hatred satisfied.

scripture.text: His disciples came, and took the body, and buried it; and they went and told Jesus.
scripture.understanding: John's grieving disciples bury his body and then go straight to Jesus with the news. In sorrow they do the one right thing: they carry their grief directly to the Lord.

scripture.text: Now when Jesus heard this, he withdrew from there in a boat, to a deserted place apart. When the multitudes heard it, they followed him on foot from the cities.
scripture.understanding: Hearing that His cousin and forerunner is dead, Jesus withdraws by boat to a solitary place — He, too, needs to grieve and pray. But the crowds pursue Him on foot, following the man of sorrows into His sorrow.

scripture.text: Jesus went out, and he saw a great multitude. He had compassion on them, and healed their sick.
scripture.understanding: Grieving Himself, Jesus steps out, sees the vast crowd, and is moved with compassion — a gut-deep mercy — and heals their sick. His own grief bends outward toward theirs; He gives from the very place He is hurting.

scripture.text: When evening had come, his disciples came to him, saying, “This place is deserted, and the hour is already late. Send the multitudes away, that they may go into the villages, and buy themselves food.”
scripture.understanding: As night falls, the disciples do the reasonable math: dismiss the crowd so they can fend for themselves. Their solution to human need is to send it away and let it become someone else's problem.

scripture.text: But Jesus said to them, “They don’t need to go away. You give them something to eat.”
scripture.understanding: Jesus overturns their logic with an impossible command: you feed them. He deliberately puts the crowd's hunger onto His disciples' empty hands — because He is about to teach them what those hands become when surrendered to Him.

scripture.text: They told him, “We only have here five loaves and two fish.”
scripture.understanding: The disciples inventory their poverty: five loaves, two fish, and the word 'only.' They measure the need against their supply and see nothing but lack.

scripture.text: He said, “Bring them here to me.”
scripture.understanding: Four words that change everything: bring what little you have to Me. The miracle does not begin with abundance; it begins with scarcity surrendered into the hands of Jesus.

scripture.text: He commanded the multitudes to sit down on the grass; and he took the five loaves and the two fish, and looking up to heaven, he blessed, broke and gave the loaves to the disciples, and the disciples gave to the multitudes.
scripture.understanding: He seats the crowd, takes the food, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks, and gives — the very rhythm He will repeat at the Last Supper. And the multiplication happens in the giving: the disciples' hands stay full only as long as they keep passing it on.

scripture.text: They all ate, and were filled. They took up twelve baskets full of that which remained left over from the broken pieces.
scripture.understanding: Everyone ate and was gorged — not merely fed but satisfied to the full — and twelve baskets of surplus remained, one for every disciple who doubted. Christ's provision does not just meet the need; it overflows it and hands the leftovers back to the ones who said 'only.'

scripture.text: Those who ate were about five thousand men, besides women and children.
scripture.understanding: Five thousand men — with women and children the number swells toward a small city — all fed from a boy's lunch. The King feeds His subjects lavishly while Herod's feast produced only a corpse.

scripture.text: Immediately Jesus made the disciples get into the boat, and to go ahead of him to the other side, while he sent the multitudes away.
scripture.understanding: Right after the miracle, Jesus compels the disciples into the boat and sends them ahead across the sea. He knowingly directs them into the path of the coming storm — obedience does not always sail into calm.

scripture.text: After he had sent the multitudes away, he went up into the mountain by himself to pray. When evening had come, he was there alone.
scripture.understanding: With the crowd dismissed, Jesus finally gets the solitude He sought at the start of the day — climbing the mountain alone to pray. Even the Son, in grief and ministry, refuels in the presence of the Father.

scripture.text: But the boat was now in the middle of the sea, distressed by the waves, for the wind was contrary.
scripture.understanding: Far from shore, the boat is battered by the waves and beaten back by a headwind. The disciples are exactly where Jesus sent them — and it is precisely there that the storm finds them.

scripture.text: In the fourth watch of the night, Jesus came to them, walking on the sea.
scripture.understanding: In the fourth watch — the blackest, most exhausted hours between three and six in the morning — Jesus comes, walking on top of the very waves that are drowning them. What terrifies them is His footpath. He treads the sea as the God who alone tramples the waves.

scripture.text: When the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were troubled, saying, “It’s a ghost!” and they cried out for fear.
scripture.understanding: When they see Him, they do not recognize deliverance — they scream that it is a ghost. In the dark, exhausted and afraid, they mistake their rescuer for a terror. Fear distorts even the coming of Christ.

scripture.text: But immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying, “Cheer up! It is I! Don’t be afraid.”
scripture.understanding: Immediately He answers their terror with His voice: Take courage — it is I — stop being afraid. 'It is I' is ego eimi, the very words God spoke from the burning bush: I AM. The One walking on the storm names Himself with the divine name.

scripture.text: Peter answered him and said, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the waters.”
scripture.understanding: Peter's faith is bold and unmistakably real: he does not want to reach Jesus by his own strength but by Jesus' word — 'command me.' He asks for the one thing that makes impossible things possible: the command of Christ.

scripture.text: He said, “Come!” Peter stepped down from the boat, and walked on the waters to come to Jesus.
scripture.understanding: One word — 'Come!' — and Peter climbs over the side and does the impossible, walking on the water toward Jesus. As long as his eyes and feet follow the word of Christ, the sea holds him up.

scripture.text: But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink, he cried out, saying, “Lord, save me!”
scripture.understanding: The instant Peter looks away from Christ to the strength of the wind, fear returns and he starts to sink. But even sinking, he prays the shortest and truest prayer in the storm: 'Lord, save me!'

scripture.text: Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand, took hold of him, and said to him, “You of little faith, why did you doubt?”
scripture.understanding: Immediately — before the lecture — Jesus' hand shoots out and seizes him. Only then comes the tender rebuke: little-faith one, why did you waver? The rescue always precedes the correction. He catches first and questions second.

scripture.text: When they got up into the boat, the wind ceased.
scripture.understanding: The moment Jesus and Peter climb in, the wind drops dead. The storm that raged all night simply ends where Christ steps aboard. His presence in the boat is the peace of the boat.

scripture.text: Those who were in the boat came and worshiped him, saying, “You are truly the Son of God!”
scripture.understanding: For the first time in Matthew, the disciples fall down and worship Jesus with a full confession of His deity: 'You are truly the Son of God.' The walk on the water and the stilled storm draw out of them the very worship due to God alone.

scripture.text: When they had crossed over, they came to the land of Gennesaret.
scripture.understanding: The crossing that nearly killed them ends safely on the far shore at Gennesaret. The storm did not stop the mission; it deepened the worship and then delivered them where He sent them.

scripture.text: When the people of that place recognized him, they sent into all that surrounding region, and brought to him all who were sick;
scripture.understanding: The moment the locals recognize Jesus, they mobilize the whole region and carry every sick person to Him. Recognition of who He is instantly becomes evangelism — they cannot keep Him to themselves.

scripture.text: and they begged him that they might just touch the fringe of his garment. As many as touched it were made whole.
scripture.understanding: They beg only to touch the tassel of His robe — and every single one who touches it is thoroughly healed. Even the hem of Jesus carries the full power to save completely; no faith that reaches for Him goes away empty.

visualMeditations.title: The Head on the Platter
visualMeditations.image: Picture the banquet hall: torchlight, wine, the laughter of powerful men, a girl still catching her breath from the dance. Then a silver serving-dish is carried in — the kind meant for roasted meat — and on it, still dripping, is the severed head of the last great prophet of Israel. The music stops. The trophy is set down before a child, who carries it to her smiling mother.
visualMeditations.meaning: This is the world's feast in one frozen image. Herod's kingdom throws a party and the centerpiece is a murdered man of God. Matthew deliberately places this banquet of death right before Jesus' banquet of bread — two kings, two tables. One serves up a corpse to save his pride; the Other serves up bread until thousands are filled. Whose table are you seated at?

visualMeditations.title: Five Loaves in the Hands of Heaven
visualMeditations.image: See Jesus standing on the green hillside, a boy's lunch in His hands — five flat barley cakes and two small dried fish, laughably little against a hillside of ten thousand hungry faces. He lifts His eyes to heaven, speaks the blessing, and begins to break. He breaks, and there is more. He hands it to a disciple, and there is still more. All night the pieces keep coming, faster than the crowd can eat, until the grass is littered with twelve full baskets of leftovers.
visualMeditations.meaning: The miracle happened in Jesus' hands and in the disciples' giving, not in the size of the lunch. Heaven does not need much from you — it needs all of what little you have, surrendered. The five loaves stayed five as long as they stayed in the disciples' anxiety; they became a feast the moment they were placed in His hands. Your 'only' is enough when it is His.

visualMeditations.title: The Figure Walking in the Fourth Watch
visualMeditations.image: It is somewhere between three and six in the morning — the fourth watch, the coldest, darkest, most hopeless stretch of the night. The disciples have been fighting the oars for hours, soaked, exhausted, going nowhere against a wall of wind. Then, out on the black water where no man can stand, a figure is walking — calmly, upright, on top of the waves that are trying to kill them. They scream. They think death itself has come striding across the sea.
visualMeditations.meaning: The thing that is drowning them is the very floor beneath His feet. What is a terror to you is a pathway to Him. And notice when He comes — not in the first watch when they still had strength, but in the fourth, at the end of themselves. He often waits until the fourth watch, not because He is absent, but because He is teaching you that the storm was never in charge.

visualMeditations.title: The Hand That Catches the Sinking Man
visualMeditations.image: Peter is up on the water, walking on impossibility, eyes locked on Jesus — and then he glances at the wind. He feels the spray, hears the roar, and the surface that held him a second ago swallows his feet. Down he goes, mouth full of seawater, three words breaking out of him: 'Lord, save me!' And instantly — no delay, no sermon first — an arm reaches down through the storm and a hand clamps around his wrist and hauls him up.
visualMeditations.meaning: Jesus lets Peter sink far enough to learn the lesson, but never far enough to drown. The rescue comes 'immediately,' before the rebuke — He catches you first and corrects you second. Little faith still had enough faith to cry out, and a three-word prayer from a sinking man is never too late. The same hand that fed thousands is the hand that grabs your wrist.

structure.label: The Martyrdom of the Forerunner (v. 1-12)
structure.body: Herod's guilty conscience, the flashback of John's arrest, and the banquet where a rash oath and wounded pride cost the greatest prophet his head.

structure.label: The Feeding of the Five Thousand (v. 13-21)
structure.body: Grieving, Jesus has compassion on the crowd, takes five loaves and two fish, and feeds thousands with twelve baskets to spare.

structure.label: The Walk on the Water (v. 22-33)
structure.body: The disciples sent into the storm, Jesus walking on the sea in the fourth watch, Peter's step of faith and sinking, and the boat's confession: 'You are truly the Son of God.'

structure.label: Healings at Gennesaret (v. 34-36)
structure.body: On the far shore the sick of the whole region reach for the fringe of His garment, and all who touch it are made completely whole.

sections.heading: Two Banquets, Two Kingdoms
paragraphs: Matthew is a master of contrast, and here he lays two feasts side by side so you cannot miss the difference between the kingdom of this world and the kingdom of heaven. Herod's banquet (v. 6-11) is a table of power, wine, lust, and pride — and it produces a severed head on a platter. Jesus' banquet (v. 15-21) is a table on the open grass, born of compassion — and it produces bread that will not run out and baskets overflowing. One king kills a prophet to protect his image in front of his guests; the other King feeds a multitude of strangers until every last one is satisfied.

That is the choice the whole chapter presses on you. The world's kingdom takes, consumes, and leaves you with death dressed up as a party. Christ's kingdom breaks, gives, multiplies, and leaves you with more than you started with. Herod is haunted the rest of his life by the man he destroyed; the disciples are handed twelve baskets by the Man who provides. You will feast at one of these two tables. The question of Matthew 14 is not whether you are hungry — it is whose bread you are eating.

sections.heading: 'It Is I': The Divine Name on the Waves
paragraphs: When Jesus calls out across the water, 'Cheer up! It is I! Don't be afraid,' the phrase 'It is I' is in Greek ego eimi — literally 'I AM.' These are the exact words the Greek Old Testament puts in God's mouth at the burning bush in Exodus 3:14, and the same self-declaration God repeats in Isaiah. Jesus is not merely identifying Himself the way a friend calls out his name in the dark; He is speaking the covenant name of God over a raging sea.

And He is doing on the water what the Old Testament says God alone can do. Job 9:8 declares that God 'alone stretches out the heavens, and treads on the waves of the sea,' and Psalm 77:19 says of God, 'Your path was through the sea... yet your footprints were unseen.' To walk on the water is a strictly divine act. So when the men in the boat fall down and cry, 'You are truly the Son of God,' they are not exaggerating — they are reading the sign correctly. The One who feeds like Yahweh and treads the sea like Yahweh has spoken the name of Yahweh: I AM. This is the highest confession of Jesus' deity so far in Matthew, and it is drawn out not by a sermon but by a storm.

ntConnection.heading: New Testament Connection
paragraphs: The feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle of Jesus' ministry recorded in all four Gospels — that is how central the early church understood it to be. And the Gospel of John, telling the very same event, records the sermon Jesus preached the next day to unpack it. In John 6:35 Jesus says, 'I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will not be hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty.' The five barley loaves multiplied on the grass were a living parable pointing to Himself: the true bread that God gives from heaven so that the world may eat and never hunger again.

Notice how John's account carries the same 'I AM' that Matthew records on the water. In John 6:20, in the identical storm, Jesus says, 'It is I (ego eimi); don't be afraid' — and then in John 6:35 He turns that same 'I AM' into 'I am the bread of life.' Matthew shows you the sign; John gives you the sermon. The Lord who broke five loaves for a hungry crowd and walked across a killing sea is saying to you the same thing He said to them: I AM enough. Come to Me, and you will be filled — chortazo, gorged, satisfied to the full — and you will never again feast at Herod's table of death.

lexicon.insight: This is not polite pity from a distance. The word comes from the splanchna — the inner organs, the guts — and means to be moved from deep in the bowels, to feel another's pain in your own body. What makes it staggering here is the timing: Jesus has just heard that John was beheaded, He is grieving and seeking solitude, and yet when He sees the crowd His insides turn over with mercy for them. He ministers out of the very place He is hurting. This is the God who feels your need in His own gut.

Jesus' words 'It is I' are ego eimi — 'I AM' — the covenant name God spoke at the burning bush (Exodus 3:14) and the divine self-declaration echoed all through Isaiah. Walking on the sea, doing what Job 9:8 says God alone can do, Jesus quiets the disciples' terror not just by identifying Himself but by pronouncing the name of God over the storm. The antidote to fear in the fourth watch is not calmer water; it is the great I AM speaking your name across it.

A compound word — oligos ('little') plus pistis ('faith'). It is one of Matthew's favorite words for the disciples, and it is important that it is 'little faith,' not 'no faith.' Peter did have faith — enough to leave the boat and walk on water, which none of the others dared. His problem was not the absence of faith but the shrinking of it when his eyes shifted from Christ to the wind. Jesus does not scold Peter for a faith too small to start; He asks why a faith that began so well was allowed to falter mid-step.

This verb literally means 'to stand in two ways' — to be pulled in two directions at once, wavering between two options. Peter's sinking was not caused by the size of the waves but by a divided heart: one eye on Jesus, one eye on the wind. Doubt here is not honest questioning; it is double-mindedness, trying to trust Christ and calculate the storm at the same time. The single-eyed gaze walks on water; the divided gaze sinks.

The word pictures falling prostrate before a superior, kissing the ground in homage — the posture due to God alone. In pious Jewish minds this act aimed at any mere man would be blasphemy. Yet here the disciples fall down and offer it to Jesus, joined to the confession 'You are truly the Son of God,' and He receives it without a word of protest. The stilled storm and the walk on the water pull the boat past admiration into adoration. Real encounters with Christ always end here — on your face, calling Him what He is.

holySpiritRevelation.intro: The Spirit is dealing with what you do with your grief, your scarcity, and your storms — and whether you will keep your eyes on the King when the wind is strong.

items.title: Ministering From the Place You Are Bleeding
items.body: Jesus had just lost John. He tried to withdraw to grieve, and the crowd chased Him into His sorrow — and instead of resenting them, He was moved with compassion and healed them (v. 13-14). He gave out of the very wound He came to nurse. Have you been waiting to feel whole before you serve, waiting for your own storm to pass before you help someone in theirs? The Spirit asks: what if the compassion the world most needs from you will have to flow out of the exact place you are still hurting? Will you let your grief make you tender instead of bitter?

items.title: Bring Me Your 'Only'
items.body: The disciples looked at five loaves and said 'only' (v. 17). Jesus said, 'Bring them here to Me' (v. 18) — and the leftovers outweighed the lunch. You have already counted your 'only': only this much money, only this much time, only this much talent, only this much faith. And you have concluded it is not enough for the size of what is in front of you. But nothing is small in the hands of Jesus. What is the 'only' you have been hiding because you were ashamed of how little it is? What would happen if you stopped protecting it and placed it in His hands tonight?

items.title: Why Did You Look at the Wind?
items.body: Peter walked on water — genuinely, gloriously walked on it — until he 'saw that the wind was strong' (v. 30). The waves did not change; his focus did. And the moment he began to sink, three words saved him: 'Lord, save me!' The Spirit is putting His finger on the exact instant your faith failed — not when the storm started, but when you turned your eyes from Christ to measure the storm. What is the 'strong wind' you have been staring at instead of at Jesus? And will you learn that even sinking, the shortest prayer still reaches the fastest hand?

audit.title: The Two-Tables Check
audit.body: Herod's table produced a corpse; Jesus' table produced a feast. Which banquet are you actually seated at right now? Where in your life are you feeding on the world's menu — protecting your image, keeping rash promises made to impress people, consuming instead of giving — and calling it living well?

audit.title: The 'Only' Inventory
audit.body: What is the resource you keep dismissing with the word 'only' — only my small salary, only my broken past, only my ordinary gifts, only my weak faith? Be specific. Have you refused to offer it to God because you were embarrassed by its size, forgetting that He specializes in multiplying exactly what looks too small to matter?

audit.title: The Strong-Wind Point
audit.body: Name the 'strong wind' you have been staring at — the bill, the diagnosis, the silence, the odds. Has looking at it made you begin to sink into fear and double-mindedness? At what precise moment did you stop looking at Jesus and start calculating the storm?

practices.title: Pray the Sinking Man's Prayer
practices.body: This week, the next time fear grips you and you feel yourself going under, do not compose a polished prayer. Do exactly what Peter did: cry out three words out loud — 'Lord, save me!' — and then look up, not at the wind. Practice shrinking your panic down to that one honest cry that always reaches the fastest hand. The prayer that saved Peter had no eloquence, only direction.

practices.title: Bring Your Five Loaves
practices.body: Take the one 'only' you named in the audit and physically surrender it this week. If it is money, give a specific amount you thought was too small to matter. If it is time, block one hour to serve someone. If it is a gift you think is ordinary, use it for one person in need. As you give it, say aloud: 'Lord, this is my five loaves. It is little, but it is Yours — break it and multiply it.' Then watch what His hands do with your 'only.'

prayerReflection: "Lord Jesus, You are truly the Son of God. I have watched You this chapter — grieving Your friend John, yet moved with compassion for the crowd; taking a boy's five loaves and feeding thousands with baskets to spare; walking across the very waves that were drowning Your disciples in the fourth watch of the night. I confess I have counted my life in 'onlys' — only this much faith, only this much to give — and hidden it from You because it felt too small. Today I bring it here to You. Break it. Multiply it. Feed others with it. When the wind is strong and I begin to sink, teach me to stop staring at the storm and to cry the only prayer that matters: 'Lord, save me!' Reach out Your hand and take hold of me before I go under, as You always do — rescuing first and correcting after. Speak Your name over my fear again: 'It is I. Don't be afraid.' And bring me safely to the other shore, where I fall down with the men in the boat and worship You as what You are. I want to feast at Your table, not Herod's. In Jesus' name, Amen."

storyConnections.title: Elisha and the Twenty Loaves
storyConnections.summary: A man brought the prophet Elisha twenty barley loaves and some fresh grain during a famine. Elisha said, 'Give it to the people, that they may eat.' His servant objected, 'What, should I set this before a hundred men?' — the same scarcity math the disciples used with the five loaves. But Elisha declared, 'Give the people, that they may eat; for the LORD says, They shall eat, and shall have some left over.' They ate and left some, just as Jesus' crowd was filled and left twelve baskets. Jesus is the greater Elisha, feeding not a hundred but thousands, proving that God's provision has always overflowed the servant's doubt.

storyConnections.title: Manna in the Wilderness
storyConnections.summary: When Israel was starving in a deserted place with no bread, God rained down manna from heaven each morning, and 'the people... gathered, some more, some less... he who gathered much had nothing over, and he who gathered little had no lack.' Everyone was filled. Centuries later Jesus does the same in a deserted place at evening — bread appearing where there was none, everyone satisfied, nothing wasted. This is why Jesus later calls Himself 'the bread of life' and the 'true bread from heaven': the feeding of the five thousand announces that the God who fed Israel in the wilderness is now standing on the grass in the flesh.

storyConnections.title: The Sailors Who Feared the LORD
storyConnections.summary: When a great storm threatened to break Jonah's ship apart, the terrified sailors cried out, and only when the raging sea grew calm did 'the men... feared the LORD exceedingly, and they offered a sacrifice to the LORD, and made vows.' A stilled storm turned pagan mariners into worshipers of the true God. In Matthew 14 the same pattern reaches its climax: when Jesus climbs into the boat and the wind ceases, the disciples fall down and worship, saying, 'You are truly the Son of God.' The storm that humbles men into worship in Jonah is now calmed not by throwing a prophet overboard, but by the presence of the One greater than Jonah stepping into the boat.
